item.title: A Simple ICU Ward Round Checklist Worth Repeating
item.dc:creator: ICU Team
item.description:
Structured checklists reduce missed items on busy multidisciplinary ward rounds. Many departments use a version of the FAST HUG mnemonic, and it remains a useful teaching anchor for residents new to the intensive care unit:

  • F — Feeding: is the patient adequately and safely nourished?
  • A — Analgesia: is pain being assessed and controlled?
  • S — Sedation: is the sedation target appropriate, and reviewed daily?
  • T — Thromboprophylaxis: has VTE prophylaxis been considered?
  • H — Head-of-bed elevation: is aspiration/VAP risk being minimised?
  • U — stress Ulcer prophylaxis: is it indicated, and still needed?
  • G — Glucose control: is glycaemic control within target range?

Using it well

A checklist is only useful if it prompts a genuine review rather than a box-ticking exercise. On our unit, the checklist is read aloud during the consultant-led round, with the bedside nurse and resident confirming each item against the patient in front of them — not from memory.

We will keep sharing short teaching notes like this one. If you have a topic you’d like covered, reach out to the department.

item.title: Marking World Anaesthesia Day at AKTH
item.dc:creator: Department of Anaesthesia & Intensive Care
item.description:
Every year on 16 October, the anaesthesia community marks World Anaesthesia Day, commemorating the first successful public demonstration of ether anaesthesia in 1846.

At AKTH, the department used the day to run a short in-house symposium for residents, nurse anaesthetists and theatre staff, focused on:

  1. Peri-operative patient safety checklists — reinforcing consistent use of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.
  2. Team communication — structured handover between theatre, recovery and the intensive care unit.
  3. Local data review — a short audit of anaesthesia-related adverse events over the past quarter, and what they teach us.

A shared global effort

Observances like this connect our department to the wider work of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists and the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists, both of which promote safe anaesthesia access worldwide — a reminder that safe surgery and anaesthesia remain out of reach for many patients globally, and that local diligence contributes to a much larger effort.

Thank you to every member of the peri-operative team who took part.

item.title: Welcome to the Department Blog
item.dc:creator: Department of Anaesthesia & Intensive Care
item.description:
Welcome to the new website for the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital.

This blog will carry:

  • Departmental announcements and CPD opportunities
  • Short clinical case discussions and teaching points
  • Updates from Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists (NSA) and WFSA activities relevant to our members
  • Notes from conferences, audits and quality-improvement projects
  • Personal reflections and experiences from our team.
  • A platform for residents and consultants to learn the art ans science of scientific, and technical writing, and to share their work with the wider anaesthesia community. This will help prepare them for the publication of their work in peer-reviewed journals, and to contribute to the body of knowledge in anaesthesia and intensive care.

Why this site exists

Anaesthesia and intensive care are, by nature, quiet specialties — much of our best work happens behind the drapes or at the bedside, rarely seen by the wider hospital community. This site is a small window into that work: who we are, what we do, and how we continue to learn. In many ways, anaesthesiologists are the unsung heroes of the medical profession.

We look forward to sharing more soon.
